demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I work hard at keeping busy with other things
Seeing people that I socialised with before the event

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel isolated and set apart from others
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
issues.explanation: For a 68-year-old retired patient, 'Overworking' is questionable as phrased because it implies a current work role; while keeping busy with tasks is plausible, the specific work-focused item is a poor fit to the demographic context.

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Evaluation' is hard to link coherently to the indexed trauma of unexpected death of a loved one and to the rest of the profile. It suggests social/performance concerns that are not reflected in the threat or appraisal items and does not fit the formulation's main Negative Appraisals ↔ Threat loop.

issues.item: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
issues.explanation: For trauma type of unexpected death of a loved one, 'Avoid Being Touched' is hard to explain clinically unless there is interpersonal assault or bodily violation content, which is not present elsewhere in the profile. It appears mismatched to the trauma context and to the other selected items.

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Evaluation' suggests shame about appearance/performance or social evaluative threat, but the rest of the profile centers bereavement-related guilt, isolation, and generalized danger. This strategy does not connect well to the stated trauma type or to the active appraisal-threat loop.

issues.item: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
issues.explanation: The threat items depict pervasive physical danger and inability to feel safe anywhere. In bereavement PTSD this can occur, but here the appraisals provided are mainly isolation and self-blame rather than danger-based meanings. The strong Negative Appraisals ↔ Threat loop is not well reflected because the appraisals do not explain this specific form of persistent external danger.

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Evaluation' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and the trauma type of traumatic bereavement. The other selected items center on grief-related self-blame, isolation, and generalized danger, but fear of being evaluated for appearance/performance suggests a social-evaluative concern not otherwise represented in threat, memory, triggers, or appraisals.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: 'Self-Blame' can occur after the unexpected death of a loved one, but in this profile it sits awkwardly beside the chosen maladaptive strategies and threat items. If the patient blames herself for the death, one would expect linked strategies or threat content tied to guilt, responsibility, rumination, or death-related cues; instead the profile emphasizes social withdrawal and generic unsafety, making this item insufficiently integrated with the rest.

issues.item: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
issues.explanation: 'Cannot Trust Safety' is not impossible in PTSD, but with traumatic bereavement and no trigger or memory items selected, the threat profile becomes very generalized. In combination with the social-evaluative avoidance item, it creates a mixed formulation in which the source of danger is unclear: bereavement-related guilt/loss versus broad physical danger versus fear of scrutiny. This weakens coherence across nodes given the active Negative Appraisals ↔ Threat linkage.

vignette:
Margaret is a sixty-eight-year-old retired woman who lives with her husband in the suburban home they bought forty years ago. Eighteen months ago, her thirty-nine-year-old son, David, died suddenly of a massive coronary while shoveling snow from their driveway on a Sunday morning. Margaret was in the kitchen making coffee when she heard the thud against the garage door. She found him on his back, his face already gray, the shovel still in his hand. She did not know CPR, and by the time the paramedics arrived, twenty-two minutes had passed. She has replayed those minutes countless times, each time certain that if she had checked on him sooner, if she had known what to do, if she had made him stop when she saw him out the window, she could have saved him. She had come to believe that her failure to protect him was not a matter of bad luck but a fundamental flaw in her-something essential she had lacked when it mattered most.

In the months that followed, Margaret found herself unable to sit still. The moment she stopped moving, the thoughts would press in: the image of his face, the paramedic's gentle hands on her arm, the certainty that she should have been faster. She began filling every hour with tasks-deep-cleaning closets that were already clean, reorganizing the pantry by expiration date, taking on small handyman projects around the house that she had never attempted before. She believed that if she kept moving, she could outrun the guilt, and she was certain that if she slowed down, the weight of what she had failed to do would crush her. But busyness did not bring relief. Instead, her body remained coiled, her shoulders tight, her jaw clenched even when she was alone in the house. She could not relax, not even in her own living room, because some part of her was always waiting for the next terrible thing to happen, and she was sure she would fail to prevent that too.

As weeks turned into months, Margaret stopped answering the phone when old friends called. She declined invitations to coffee, to book club, to the neighborhood potluck. Seeing people she had socialized with before David's death became unbearable-not because she disliked them, but because she was certain they saw her differently now, as the woman who had let her son die. She felt isolated and set apart from others, and she had come to believe that she no longer belonged anywhere, not even among people who had known her for decades. The more she withdrew, the more her body stayed on alert, her heart racing at the sound of a phone ringing or a doorbell she was not expecting, her mind scanning every room for signs of danger even though she knew, logically, that she was safe. She had become convinced that her failure was visible, that others could see it in her face, and that the only way to protect herself from their judgment was to stay away. But staying away only deepened her sense that she was fundamentally different from everyone else, and that difference felt like a threat she could not escape.

Margaret's husband tried to coax her out of the house, but she resisted. She had begun to feel that even he must see her differently now, that he must blame her in some quiet way he would never say aloud. She avoided sitting with him in the evenings, afraid that if they talked too long, the subject of David would come up, and she would have to hear the accusation she was sure was there. Her body remained tense through the night, her sleep fractured, her muscles rigid even as she lay beside him. The isolation she felt had become a kind of second skin, and the more she withdrew, the more her body stayed locked in a state of readiness, as though danger were always just around the corner.

What finally brought Margaret to seek help was a moment of quiet terror. She was alone in the house on a Sunday morning, the same day of the week David had died, and she heard a thud from the garage. It was only a box of old books her husband had dropped, but for ten seconds she could not breathe, her heart pounding so hard she thought she might collapse. She realized then that she could not go on this way, that her body and her mind had become a trap she could not escape. She is most afraid that nothing will change, that she will spend the rest of her life feeling this way, and that the guilt she carries will never lift. But she is also afraid of what it might mean to let it go.
